subject.title: Circle Poems
subject.author: Lew Welch
subject.text:
Whenever I have a day off, I write a new poem.
Does this mean you shouldn't work, or that you
write best on your day off?
 
For example, this is the poem I wrote today.
 
 
                                     *
 
 
When he was 20, he understood some of the secrets of
life, and undertook to write them down so simply that
even an idiot could understand.
"For," he reasoned, "if I can't do that, I don't
understand it myself."
 
He proved himself right.
When he was 50, he didn't understand it himself.
 
 
                                      *
 
 
"Why is it," he said, "that no matter what you say,
a woman always takes it personally?"
 
"I never do," she said.
 
 
                                      *
 
 
John said, "Then I met that short fat guy with the
neat little beard, with a name like dawn."
 
"You mean George Abend?"
 
"Yeah."
 
"Abend means evening."

 
                                     *

title: The Man Who Understood Everything at Twenty
standfirst: Lew Welch's "Circle Poems" strings together small, overheard ironies about people who contradict themselves without noticing. Read against what happened to him in 1971, the poem's own joke about a man who understands less as he ages stops sounding like a joke.

sections.heading: A Man Who Understood Everything at Twenty
sections.body:
Buried in the middle of "Circle Poems" is a two-sentence biography of nobody in particular:

> When he was 20, he understood some of the secrets of
> life, and undertook to write them down so simply that
> even an idiot could understand.
>
> He proved himself right.
> When he was 50, he didn't understand it himself.

It reads as a throwaway joke on first pass, one of several small anecdotes Lew Welch strings together under a title that never explains itself. Welch was 44 when he walked out of a friend's house in the Sierra foothills in May 1971 carrying a borrowed pistol and was never seen again. He did not make it to 50. Whether he wrote this particular fragment as a joke about someone else or about his own drift is not recoverable from the text — but a poet who spent his life editing his own thought down to plain speech, and then disappeared into a mountain range with a suicide note that explained almost nothing, makes the line hard to read as pure comedy.

sections.heading: Three Very Small Jokes, Each Contradicting Itself
sections.body:
The poem is built from a handful of these vignettes, none longer than a few lines, separated by asterisks like entries in a notebook. Two others sit either side of the aging joke. In one, a man complains, "Why is it that no matter what you say, a woman always takes it personally?" "I never do," she said — a reply that disproves itself in the act of making it, since taking an accusation personally enough to deny it is exactly what she has just done.

In the other, John describes meeting "that short fat guy with the / neat little beard, with a name like dawn." His friend supplies the name: George Abend. *Abend* is German for evening — the opposite of dawn, and the joke depends entirely on the reader knowing it. Every fragment in the sequence works the same way: someone states a thing confidently and the poem quietly hands you the detail that undoes it. That is presumably the circle of the title — not a shape on the page, but a shape statements make when they curve back and catch their speaker out.

sections.heading: "Write Like You Talk"
sections.body:
Welch arrived at Reed College in Portland in 1948 and roomed with Gary Snyder, later becoming close with Philip Whalen — the three would be grouped together for the rest of their careers. He had discovered Gertrude Stein at Stockton Junior College and wrote his Reed thesis on her; when William Carlos Williams visited campus and read the students' work, he singled out Welch's poems and tried, without success, to get the Stein thesis into print.

That early apprenticeship in plain, repetitive, spoken-sounding sentences stayed with him. From 1965 to 1970 he taught a poetry workshop through UC Extension in San Francisco under a motto simple enough to fit on a poster: *write like you talk*. "Circle Poems," with its overheard dialogue and its shrug of an opening line — "this is the poem I wrote today" — is that principle with almost nothing else added. His best-known piece, "Chicago Poem," drew praise from Marianne Moore, a rare mainstream nod for a poet who spent most of his career next to two more famous roommates.

sections.heading: Raid Kills Bugs Dead, and Other Ways to Pay Rent
sections.body:
Poetry did not pay, so Welch worked: as a copywriter in Chicago and then at Montgomery Ward's advertising department, as a New York adman, later as a San Francisco cab driver, a longshoreman's clerk and a commercial fisherman. He is sometimes credited with writing the slogan "Raid Kills Bugs Dead," a claim biographers treat with some skepticism but which has followed him into most short accounts of his life regardless.

The domestic detail that outlasts the advertising trivia is this: Welch lived for years with Magdalena Cregg, a Polish refugee, and helped raise her son, Hugh — who grew up to front Huey Lewis and the News. A Beat poet who wrote spare, plainspoken elegies for the natural world was, for a stretch of the 1960s, also the stepfather of the future co-writer of "The Power of Love."

sections.heading: "Lew, You'll Never Change"
sections.body: In May 1971 Welch was staying at Gary Snyder's home on the San Juan Ridge north of Nevada City, building a cabin on land Allen Ginsberg had deeded him nearby. On a walk, he shot a lizard with a pistol; Snyder rebuked him for it, reportedly telling him, "Lew, you'll never change." Welch took a .22 revolver from Snyder's footlocker and walked off. His van was found later with a note inside — he had "used it all up," it said, and "went Southwest." No body was ever recovered. A search involving Snyder, students and neighbouring communes ran for days and turned up nothing; an unverified sighting at a Nevada City bank a week later was enough for the county to file him as missing rather than declare a suicide. Biographers still give his death year with a question mark.

sections.heading: A Question the Poem Already Asked
sections.body: "Circle Poems" opens by wondering about its own conditions of production — "Whenever I have a day off, I write a new poem. / Does this mean you shouldn't work, or that you / write best on your day off?" — before shrugging the question aside: "this is the poem I wrote today." It is a poet noting, without much ceremony, that today happened to produce this. Welch's last known act reads uncomfortably like the same gesture scaled up: a man who walked out of a house on an ordinary spring morning and simply did not come back, leaving behind a note that gestured at a direction rather than a reason. The poem never claims to know why any of its three strangers say what they say. It only shows the moment the ground shifts under them. Its author got the same moment, and nobody has ever found where it led.
